title: Polynomial-time equivalence of free binary decision diagrams
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for equivalence of two explicitly given free binary decision diagrams? In full quantifiers, are there a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), constants \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid pair \((B_1,B_2)\), of total binary encoding length \(L\), the machine halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and returns YES exactly when \[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_{B_1}(a)=f_{B_2}(a),\] where \(X\) is the union of the variable labels appearing in the two inputs? No shared variable order is promised.
why: FBDDs allow different branches to choose different variable orders and can be much more compact than ordered diagrams. Reliable equivalence testing is needed to compare independently compiled representations or optimized versions of a Boolean function. The question asks whether that representational flexibility can coexist with deterministic exact polynomial-time comparison, beyond the known randomized guarantee.
status_note: Darwiche–Marquis 2002 mark FBDD equivalence as unknown; the checked Darwiche–Huang theorem supplies a randomized one-sided polynomial-time test. The 2026 proof-system discussion concerns stronger join verification and different structured formats, not a checked resolution of two-FBDD deterministic equivalence. A bounded primary-source search through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; source-open records the dated question, not exhaustive present-status certification.

sentences: A free binary decision diagram tests each Boolean variable at most once along a path while allowing the order to vary between paths.
The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can decide equivalence of any two such diagrams in polynomial time in their explicit encodings.
Equivalence requires agreement on every assignment, even when the diagrams use unrelated variable orders.
A one-sided randomized polynomial-time test is known, while hardness for more demanding diagram operations does not settle this exact comparison task.
A deterministic resolution would clarify how much compact representation can be retained while supporting reliable exact comparison of Boolean functions.

definitions:
A free binary decision diagram (FBDD) is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph. Each nonterminal vertex is labelled by a Boolean variable and has exactly two outgoing edges, one marked 0 and one marked 1; their targets may coincide. A terminal vertex has no outgoing edge and is labelled by the output bit 0 or 1. All vertices can be taken reachable from the root. On every directed root-to-terminal path, each variable occurs at most once. Different paths, and the two different input diagrams, may inspect variables in different orders. In particular no fixed global linear order or common graph ordering is part of the input. Redundant tests and shared subgraphs are permitted; the diagrams need not be reduced or isomorphic.

For an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\), start at the root and at a vertex labelled \(x\) follow its edge marked \(a(x)\); acyclicity leads to a terminal, whose label is \(f_B(a)\). Variables absent from a diagram do not affect its value. Constant diagrams consisting of one terminal and the case \(X=\varnothing\) are included. The input is an explicit finite vertex table giving the root, each node's type and label, and its two successor indices when present. Identifiers, labels and indices are binary encoded, and \(L\) counts all bits in both tables. Inputs are promised to meet the graph and path conditions. All arithmetic, preprocessing and reading costs belong to the ordinary sequential deterministic bit-time bound; no unit-cost manipulation of unbounded integers, oracle, random coins or nonuniform advice is allowed. One program and one polynomial work for all pairs. Correctness is exact on every assignment, not agreement on most assignments or numerical approximation. Only the YES/NO equivalence answer is required; canonicalization or construction of a combined diagram is not an additional output.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that such a uniform polynomial-time equivalence decider exists, including the graph semantics, input encoding, runtime and both correctness directions, or prove the negation of the displayed quantified claim. The negative target rules out every deterministic polynomial-time machine on the promised FBDD input class; failure of one graph comparison or one representation-conversion method is insufficient. A randomized polynomial-time test or a deterministic test requiring a common ordering does not meet the full target. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional version unless its premise is proved. This review supplies no Lean proof of either answer.

context_blocks.text: An FBDD records a branching computation that tests a variable at most once on each path. It generalizes an ordered binary decision diagram by allowing the order to vary between branches. Shared subgraphs make its explicit representation potentially much smaller than the full truth table.

Darwiche–Marquis Table 5 marks equivalence for FBDDs as unknown. This is distinct from entailment between diagrams and from constructing their conjunction; the map treats these as separate operations. The card retains equivalence alone.

Darwiche–Huang give randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing for FBDDs and even for general d-DNNFs. For every fixed equivalent pair the test accepts with certainty; for every fixed inequivalent pair it incorrectly accepts with probability at most one half. This is the one-sided-error class coRP, and their bit-length analysis makes the polynomial-time claim an ordinary finite-arithmetic claim.

That error statement is conditioned on the fixed input, not a posterior probability that the input is equivalent after a positive answer. The source’s informal confidence wording is therefore expressed here as the precise one-sided algorithmic guarantee. The requested deterministic answer admits no such error.

The 2026 structured-circuit paper discusses hardness of verifying a join rule for FBDDs: testing whether a third represented function equals the conjunction of two others. That is a different, three-diagram operation. Its hardness is not presented as a lower bound for the two-diagram equivalence question.

Every FBDD has a polynomial-size translation into deterministic decomposable negation normal form. Thus a deterministic general d-DNNF equivalence algorithm would also solve this card; an FBDD-only algorithm would not by itself settle that broader question. The related cards retain those different targets.

The September 2026 bounded search checked the foundational map, the randomized theorem and the newer proof-system discussion, without finding a matching deterministic solution or impossibility theorem. The dated unknown table cell is not an exhaustive certificate of present openness.
